title: Lists: ArrayList
summary: A list that grows as you add to it, and why it holds Integer instead of int.

say.never: An array is a row of boxes, and you pick how many when you make it. That's a problem when you don't know how many things are coming, like songs added to a playlist. An **ArrayList** is a list that grows: `add` puts a new item on the end, `size()` tells you how many there are, and `get(0)` reads the first one.
say.bit: An **ArrayList** grows as you `add`. `size()` counts the items; `get(i)` reads one by index.

say.never: The type in the angle brackets says what the list holds. Lists can only hold **objects**, and `int` is a plain number, not an object. So Java gives every plain type an object twin: `Integer` for `int`, `Double` for `double`. You write `ArrayList<Integer>`, then add and read plain `int`s; Java wraps and unwraps them for you. That's called **boxing**.
say.bit: Collections hold objects, so write `Integer`, not `int`. Java boxes and unboxes for you.

say.never: `ArrayList` isn't part of the core language. It lives in Java's library, in a package called `java.util`. An `import` line at the very top of the file tells Java where to find it. `import java.util.*;` brings in everything from that package at once.
say.bit: `import java.util.ArrayList;` at the top of the file, or `import java.util.*;` for all of it.

steps.title: In your lesson: A list that grows

say.never: `ScoreList` keeps one team's match scores in an `ArrayList<Integer>` called `scores_`. Import it at the top, add the field, and then `addScore` is one line and `count()` just returns the list's size.
say.bit: Import `ArrayList`, add `scores_`, then `addScore` adds and `count()` returns `size()`.

say.never: A **for-each loop** works on a list just like on an array. `for (int lap : lap_seconds)` reads as "for each lap in lap_seconds". It visits the items in order, with no index to count. You can loop with plain `int` even though the list holds `Integer`s.
say.bit: `for (int lap : lap_seconds)` visits every item in order.

steps.title: In your lesson: Visiting every item

say.never: `average()` adds every score with a for-each loop and divides by `scores_.size()`. Cast the total to `double` first, or the decimals vanish. `best()` starts with `scores_.get(0)` and keeps the biggest. Both have to check `scores_.isEmpty()` first, because an empty list has no item 0 and you can't divide by zero.
say.bit: `average()`: total ÷ size, as a `double`. `best()`: keep the biggest. Check `isEmpty()` first.
